Chapter 7: Reproductive Endocrinology

 eproductive Physiology: The Ovary and Testes— R Anatomy and Physiology

The mature ovaries are paired nodular structures having 2.5–5/2/1 cm, while normal adult ♂ testicular volume is around 18.6 ± 4.8 mL. The two major functions of the adult gonads:

• The synthesis and secretion of sex steroids

• Gametogenesis

The components of the ovarian follicle are the theca cells, the granulosa cells, and the primary oocyte. The theca cells produce androgens, and the granulosa cells produce estrogens. The other stromal cells that contribute to androgen production can be divided into the secondary interstitial cells (derived from theca) and the hilum cells. The testes contain two major components that are structurally separated and serve different functions: the Leydig cells, or interstitial cells, comprise the major endocrine component and the seminiferous tubules that make up 90% of testicular volume. The following are the three important cells of the testes and ovaries, respectively:

• Interstitial cells: ♂ Leydig cells, ♀ theca cells—which are found in between the

seminiferous tubules and follicles, respectively. Produce androgens under LH drive.

• Cells supporting gametogenesis: ♂ Sertoli cells, ♀ granulosa cells—secrete

estrogens and other hormones, including inhibin and Müllerian inhibitory factor (AMH) under FSH drive. The former inhibits FSH secretion from the pituitary gland, and the latter–AMH, when secreted by Sertoli cells, is responsible for suppressing ♀ sex organ development during sexual differentiation in utero. In adult ♀, AMH is produced in proportion to germ cell number and is, therefore, a marker of ovarian ageing. © Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2020 I. R. The Sertoli cells also secrete androgen-binding protein (ABP), a molecule with high affinity for androgens. This substance, which enters the tubular lumen, provides a high concentration of testosterone to the developing germinal cells during the process of spermatogenesis.

• Germ cells: ♂ continue to make new germ cells throughout adult life in the basal

membrane of tubules. ♀ cease to make new germ cells after birth and are, therefore, born with all of the “eggs” that they will ever make. Functional units:

• ♂ Seminiferous tubules. Spermatogenesis occurs here in the presence of high

intratesticular concentrations of testosterone. Made up of germ cells and Sertoli cells that line the basement membrane and form tight junctions with other Sertoli cells, establishing a blood–testis barrier, through which spermatogonia mature to be released into the lumen of the tubule.

• ♀ Graafian follicle. Primordial follicles are recruited in batches, mature over

2 months, with selection of a dominant follicle with single central oocyte surrounded by granulosa cells which convert theca-derived testosterone to estradiol (under the influence of aromatase expressed by these cells) for ovulation. Follicles which do not proceed to ovulation become atretic.

 he Regulation of Gonadal Function: The T Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis

7.1.1.1 Hypothalamus

Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) is secreted by the hypothalamus in a pulsatile manner (every 30–120 min) in response to stimuli from the cerebral cortex and limbic system via various neurotransmitters, for example, leptin, kisspeptin, endorphins, catecholamines, and dopamine. GnRH release initially occurs during sleep in early puberty and then throughout the day in adulthood. It stimulates the secretion of LH and FSH by the pituitary gland. The pattern of GnRH secretion is crucial for normal gonadotrophin secretion. Faster pulse frequencies are essential for LH secretion, whereas slower frequencies favor FSH secretion; continuous administration of GnRH abolishes both LH and FSH secretion. In addition, in ♀ cyclic, predictable menses require the pulsatile release of LHRH (GnRH) within a critical range of frequencies: approximately 90 min during early follicular phase, 60–70 min during late follicular phase, 100 min during early luteal phase and 200 min during late luteal phase → this variation is responsible for changes in FSH, LH levels, and ovarian steroid release during the phases of the menstrual cycle (Figs. 7.1 and 7.3).

7.1.1.2 Pituitary

• LH drives interstitial cell synthesis and secretion of testosterone (Fig. 7.2) in

both sexes and triggers ovulation in ♀. Negative feedback by sex steroids.

• FSH in ♂ drives Sertoli cell-mediated sperm maturation and production of seminiferous tubule fluid as well as a number of substances thought to be important

for spermatogenesis and inhibin. FSH in ♀ drives granulosa cell-mediated aromatization of androgens to estradiol. Negative feedback mainly by inhibin (+ steroids). An intrapituitary network involving several factors, including activin that enhances FSH, plays a role in regulating gonadotropin synthesis and secretion (Fig. 7.1).

7.1.1.3 The Gonads Hormones

The Ovary

In ♀, estradiol rises with follicle maturation under FSH drive of granulosa cells (during the follicular phase) (Fig. 7.3). Estradiol is also made by the placenta and corpus luteum as well as by the conversion of androgens precursors in other tissues (e.g., adipose tissue), which is clinically important after the menopause and in some women with disorders of ovarian function.

Progesterone secreted from corpus luteum (during the luteal phase), which is derived from granulosa cells, only after ovulation occurs. Peak production on day 21 of a 28-day cycle. Ovaries also secrete testosterone and other androgens which either serve as precursors to estrogen synthesis—the theca cells, which lack aromatase, synthesize androgens (mainly androstenedione) which diffuse into the granulosa cells (which lack 17 hydroxylase) where they are used for estrogen production or are released into the circulation to act on peripheral tissues.

The Testes

In ♂, testosterone and small amounts of DHEA sulfate and DHT are produced by Leydig cells. ♂ testosterone has a circadian rhythm, with maximum secretion at around 8 a.m. and minimum around 9 p.m.

7.1.2 Regulation of Gametogenesis

• Both FSH and LH are required for gametogenesis.

• FSH, through its action on Sertoli and granulosa cells, is vital for sperm and

oocyte maturation.

• FSH is necessary for the initiation of spermatogenesis; however, full maturation

of the spermatozoa appears to require not only an FSH effect but also testosterone.

• LH ensures high intragonadal concentrations of testosterone (exogenous testosterone cannot substitute).

• ♂: the whole process of spermatogenesis (spermatogonia → I spermatocytes →

II spermatocytes → spermatids → spermatozoa) takes approximately 74 days, followed by another 12–21 days for sperm transport through the epididymis.

• ♀: from primordial follicle to primary follicle, it takes about 180 days (a continuous process). It is then another 60 days to form a preantral follicle which then

proceeds to ovulation three menstrual cycles later. Only the last 2–3 weeks of this process is under gonadotrophin drive, during which time the follicle grows from 2 to 20 mm.

7.1.3 Androgen Action

• Both testosterone and DHT exert their activity by binding to androgen receptors,

the latter more avidly than testosterone.

• ♂ sexual differentiation during embryogenesis.

• Development and maintenance of ♂ sex characteristics after puberty.

7.1.4 Estrogen Action

• Estradiol binds to A (reproductive tissues) and B (bone, brain, heart, etc.)

receptors.

• Development of ♀ sex characteristics.

• ⊕ stromal development and ductal growth in the breast.

• Increase fat stores.

• Increase vaginal wall and uterine thickening.

• Cervix: ⊕ production of large amounts of thin watery mucus, through which

sperm can penetrate most readily.

7.1.5 Progesterone Action

• Converts the endometrium to its secretory stage to prepare the uterus for

implantation.

• Affects the vaginal epithelium and cervical mucus, making it thick and impenetrable to sperm.

• Glandular development of the breasts.

• ↑ the body temperature in humans.

7.1.6 Menstrual Cycle

The ovary has two phases: the follicular phase and the luteal phase. The endometrium has three phases and is synchronized by the ovary. The complex feedback loops between the ovary and the HP axis regulate the menstrual cycle. During the follicular phase, the ovary secretes estradiol, which stimulates the endometrium to undergo proliferative phase. After ovulation (luteal phase) the ovary secretes estrogen and progesterone, which maintains the endometrial lining and promotes the secretory phase. In a nonpregnant cycle, luteolysis occurs, resulting in cessation of hormone production. This hormone withdrawal results in the degenerative phase and the onset of menses (Fig. 7.3).

 enstrual Function Disorders: Assessment M and Investigation

7.2.1 Definitions

• Primary amenorrhea = failure of menarche by the age of 16 years.

• Secondary amenorrhea = the cessation of menses for >6 months in ♀ who had

previously menstruated or no menses for more than three cycles in an individual who has previously had cyclic menses.

• Oligomenorrhea is defined as the reduction in the frequency of menses to <9

periods a year. The causes of amenorrhea are grouped according to the level of involvement in the regulatory system that governs normal menstrual activity (i.e., hypothalamic, pituitary, ovarian, and uterine). If the outflow tract is intact (uterus and vagina present), amenorrhea is most likely the result of disruption in the HPO axis.

Ovarian Insufficiency or ♀ Hypogonadism

7.3.1 Definition

Ovarian insufficiency also termed hypogonadism is defined as diminished functional activity of the ovaries—that may result in diminished production of sex hormones.

7.3.2 Classification of ♀ Hypogonadism (Ovarian Insufficiency)

Insufficiency)

• Secondary/central hypogonadism (this is usually caused by diseases of the pituitary

Note: POI/POF is a disorder characterized by amenorrhea, estrogen deficiency, and elevated gonadotrophins, developing in ♀ <40 years, as a result of loss of ovarian follicular function. 7.3.2.1 Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea

Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea is one of the most common types of amenorrhea and accounts for 15–35% of cases. It is an endocrine disorder, although the exact mechanism has not been definitively determined. It is characterized by a reduced GnRH drive (decrease in pulse frequency and amplitude), leading to low or low-normal serum levels of FSH and LH and resulting in anovulation. The ratio of serum FSH to LH in these patients is often equivalent to that of a prepubertal female with a relative FSH dominance (FSH-LH ratio >1 in the presence of hypoestrogenemia). Hypothalamic dysfunction has been observed in female athletes. Competitors in events such as gymnastics, ballet, marathon running, and diving can show menstrual irregularities ranging from luteal phase defects to amenorrhea. Hypothalamic dysfunction and functional hypothalamic amenorrhea have been described also in association with eating disorders. Anorexia nervosa is a disorder characterized by relentless dieting in pursuit of a thin body habitus. Approximately 95% of cases occur in females, and the onset is chiefly in adolescence. The clinical features include extreme weight loss leading to a body weight less than 85% of normal for age and height, a distorted body image, intense fear of gaining weight, a preoccupation with food, with an obsessive-compulsive personality. The associated symptoms include hypothermia, mild bradycardia, dry skin, constipation, and symptoms of hypoestrogenemia. Bulimia occurs in about half of patients with anorexia and is defined as binge eating followed by self-induced purging. These patients also have a variety of neuroendocrine aberrations—often to a lesser degree than those with anorexia—which also lead to menstrual disturbances.

History and Physical Examination

• Manifestations of estrogen deficiency, for example, hot flushes, reduced libido,

and dyspareunia.

• Hypothalamic dysregulation, for example, exercise and nutritional history, body

weight changes, BMI, emotional stress, recent or chronic physical illness.

• In primary amenorrhea—history of breast development, history of cyclical pain,

age of menarche of mother and sisters.

• In secondary amenorrhea—duration and regularity of previous menses, family

history of early menopause or familial autoimmune disorders.

• Secondary sex characteristics.

• Anosmia may indicate Kallmann’s syndrome.

• Hirsutism or acne, evidence of hyperandrogenism or virilization.

• Galactorrhea, visual field defects.

• History or evidence suggestive of pituitary, thyroid, or adrenal dysfunction.

• Drug history—for example, causes of hyperprolactinemia, chemotherapy, hormonal contraception.

• Obstetric and surgical history.

• Features of Turner’s syndrome or other dysmorphic features.

7.3.5.1 Treatment of Ovarian Insufficiency with Prepubertal Onset

Sex Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT)

• Exogenous estrogens are required to compensate estrogen deficiency

The goals of HRT in young adolescents: To develop and maintain secondary sexual characteristics, mainly breast development and feminization, to induce growth spurt, to induce bone mass acquisition and to maintain bone mass. Estrogens can be administered as 17β-E2, estradiol valerate (EV), conjugated estrogens, or ethinyl estradiol (EE). E2 is the endogenous estrogen. In Europe, it is available in the form of a pill, transdermal (TD) patches and gel. EV is a synthetic prodrug of 17β-E2. After oral administration, it is rapidly hydrolyzed to E2 by intestinal enzymes. Conjugated equine estrogens (CEE) are extracted from equine urine and contain more than 100 estrogenic compounds of different potencies.

Ovarian Insufficiency or ♀ Hypogonadism

157

The main estrogens contained in CEE are E2, estrone (E1), and estriol (E3). CEE is used mainly in the United States for postmenopausal treatment. Historically, it has been the most widely used form of estrogen for the induction of puberty in the United States. EE is a synthetic estrogen, being the main estrogen used in combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs). Concerning the route of E2 administration, several studies illustrated that TD 17β-E2 is more physiological than oral 17β-E2. Estrogens should initially be administered alone, and the dosage should be increased progressively, in order to mimic natural puberty. For example, a usual regimen starts with EE2 5 μg/day ↑ to 10–20 μg/day or CEE 0.3–0.625 mg/day on days 1–21 of the month (or from day 1 to day 25 of the month); 10 mg of medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA)/dydrogesterone are then added on days 12–21 (or from day 12–14 to day 25) after physical signs of estrogen effect are noted and breakthrough bleeding occurs (and always within 6 months after initiating estrogen); no treatment is given between day 25 and the end of the month. Withdrawal bleedings usually occur within a few days after stopping the treatment. This will recreate the physiology of the menstrual cycle; later the patient may be switched to oral contraceptives, which are more convenient and preferred by most adolescents, although TD 17β-E2 with oral progesterone probably represents the most physiological route for HRT. If there is a coexisting GH deficiency (in the setting of pituitary failure) first treat de GH deficiency, then add estrogen replacement therapy. When the diagnosis of hypogonadism is made in childhood, the optimal age at which to start is around the age of 12. The duration of HRT is recommended up to the age of physiological menopause, on average at 50–51 years. The contraindications to HRT are illustrated in Table 7.2.

7.3.5.2 Treatment of Ovarian Insufficiency with Postpubertal Onset

Hormone replacement therapy (estrogens and progesterone) is essential in premenopausal women. The goals of HRT: To maintain secondary sex characteristics (e.g., vulvar and vaginal lubrication), to prevent osteoporosis, to abolish vasomotor symptoms with an improvement in sense of well-being. Furthermore, HRT protects against cardiovascular risk. Estrogens and progestins can be administered in a sequential scheme or as a continuous regimen.   e.g. CYCLO-PROGYNOVA® (21 tb) Estradiol valerat 2 mg (11 tb) and estradiol valerat 2 mg + norgestrel 0.5 mg (10 tb)    FEMOSTON® 2/10 or 1/10 (28 tb) Estradiol (2 mg/1 mg) 14 tb + estradiol (2 mg/1 mg and dydrogesterone) 14 tb

Estrogens may only be administered alone, in the absence of progesterone or progestins, in adolescents or women without a uterus. Topical (for use on skin): patch, gel/orally. GnRH or FSH+ LH stimulation treatment if fertility is desired (in secondary (central) ovarian insufficiency).

7.4 Menopause

7.4.1 Definition

Relative—seek advice

• Past history of endometrial cancer

• Family or past history of thromboembolism

• Ischemic heart disease

• Cerebrovascular disease

• Active liver disease

• Hypertriglyceridemia

The menopause is the permanent cessation of menstruation as a result of ovarian failure and is a retrospective diagnosis made after 12 months of amenorrhea. It is characterized by morphological and structural changes in the body, mainly resulting from the loss of estrogen production. There is a progressive decline in ovarian function over a period of 15 years. The menopausal transition ends with the final menstrual period, which cannot be recognized until after 12 months of amenorrhea. The average age of ♀ at the time of the menopause is 50–51 years (46–55 years). Early menopause or premature ovarian failure refers to menopause prior <40 years (1%). The perimenopause encompasses the menopause transition and the first year following the last menstrual period.

7.4.2 Long-Term Menopausal Consequences

Vasomotor symptoms and urogenital atrophy, osteoporosis, atherosclerotic disease and ischemic heart disease, dementia.

7.4.3 Clinical Presentation of Menopause

• Menstrual disturbances (90%).

• Hot flushes often associated with sweats and skin flushing.

• Urinary symptoms and sexual dysfunction: atrophy of urethral and bladder

mucosa and vaginal atrophy may result in urinary incontinence, an ↑ risk of urinary tract infections and dyspareunia and vaginal dryness, respectively; ↓ sexual arousal and libido.

• Mood changes: anxiety, forgetfulness, difficulty in concentration, and irritability

have all been attributed to the menopause.

Menopause

7.4.4 Evaluation of Menopause

(e.g., if HRT is being considered) • • • •

7.4.4.1 History

Perimenopausal symptoms and their severity. Assess risk factors for cardiovascular disease (CVD) and osteoporosis. Assess risk factors for breast cancer and thromboembolic disease. History of active liver disease.

7.4.5 Investigations

FSH levels fluctuate markedly in the perimenopausal period and correlate poorly with symptoms. When a woman’s FSH blood level is consistently elevated to 40 mIU/mL or higher (e.g., FSH > 40 UI/L on two different occasions), and she has not had a menstrual period for a year, it is generally accepted that she has reached menopause. Others: E2 ↓< 20 pg/mL; AMH ↓.

7.4.6 Menopause Treatment Considerations

The aim of treatment of perimenopausal ♀ is to alleviate menopausal symptoms and optimize quality of life.

7.4.6.1 Benefits of HRT

Hot flushes, urinary symptoms, vaginal atrophy, osteoporosis respond well to estrogen therapy. Long-term use of HRT in older menopausal women has been associated with increased risks for venous thromboembolism, coronary events, stroke, and breast cancer. Although short-term treatment of symptomatic women during the menopausal transition likely poses significantly fewer risks, HRT generally should be used in the lowest effective dose and for the shortest time required (e.g., conjugated equine estrogens 0.3 mg/day can achieve an almost 75% reduction in vasomotor symptoms over 12 weeks).

7.4.6.2 Alternatives to HRT

→ Concerns about the risks of HRT have ↑ interest in nonhormonal alternatives for the treatment of symptoms in the menopausal transition. Herbal treatments—hot flushes. Neuroactive agents, including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) (e.g., fluoxetine), serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) (e.g., venlafaxine, alpha adrenergic agents, and others) all have some efficacy in the treatment of vasomotor symptoms.

7.5 Hirsutism

7.5.1 Definition

Hirsutism is excessive terminal hair (thick or dark hair) that appears in a male pattern (excessive hair in androgen-dependent areas; that is, sexual hair, mustache, beard, central chest, shoulders, lower abdomen, back, inner thigh) in women as a result of ↑ androgen production and ↑ skin sensitivity to androgens (Table 7.3). It may be accompanied by other evidence of androgen excess, such as acne, oily skin and hair, and male pattern alopecia. Hypertrichosis is a separate condition. It is distributed in a generalized, nonsexual pattern (i.e., predominantly on forearms or lower legs); it may be hereditary or result from certain medications (e.g., phenytoin, cyclosporine). The Ferriman–Gallwey score is used to assess the extent and the degree of hirsutism, evaluating hair growth in nine regions of the body (most sensitive to androgen). This provides a semi-objective method of monitoring disease progression and treatment outcome. Generalized hirsutism (score >8) is abnormal in the general US population and needs evaluation especially when menstrual irregularity is present as well.

Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

The majority of hirsutism is due to androgen excess (>80%), and the majority of women with hirsutism (70–80%) have PCOS.

7.6.1 Definition

PCOS is a syndrome defined by the presence of a combination of at least two out of three of the following (according to 2003 Rotterdam criteria, in widespread use):

• Otherwise unexplained chronic hyperandrogenism (clinical or biochemical)

• Oligoovulation

• Ultrasonographic polycystic ovarian morphology

It’s considered the most common endocrinopathy of women of reproductive age. PCOS is a complex endocrine condition, due to its heterogeneity and uncertainty about its etiology. There are a lot of debates on the definition of PCOS. Hence, based on the available data, the AE-PCOS Society Task Force proposed in 2006 that PCOS should be defined by the presence of:

• Clinical (hirsutism = male-pattern hair growth in ♀) and/or biochemical hyperandrogenemia

• Chronic oligo/anovulation (oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea) OR polycystic ovarian

morphology

• Exclusion of other androgen excess and related disorders that may result in ovulatory

dysfunction, including hyperprolactinemia and thyroid abnormalities

7.6.2 Features

Oligo-/amenorrhea (70%) due to anovulation, hirsutism, seborrhea, and/or acne, and androgenic alopecia or male pattern balding, insulin resistance, overweight/ obesity, ± infertility.

7.6.3 Investigations of PCOS

The aims of investigations are mainly to exclude serious underlying disorders and to screen for complications, as the diagnosis is primarily clinical. Testosterone may be ↑ (performed primarily as a screen for the presence of other causes of hyperandrogenism), SHBG ↓ (owing to the hyperinsulinemic state, with a

• Weight loss in obese ♀ with PCOS will improve insulin sensitivity and significantly reduce hyperandrogenemia.

and hirsutism, or

• Cyclical progestogen: Cerazette® (desogestrel), a progesterone-only contraceptive pill with minimal androgenic properties when estrogens are contraindicated.

Pharmacological treatment of hirsutism is directed at slowing the growth of new hair. It should be combined with mechanical methods of hair removal, such as electrolysis and laser therapy. It includes combined oral contraceptive pill and androgen receptor blockers, which are most effective when used in combination.

• Metformin: in obese women and those with insulin resistance.

7.7 Turner Syndrome (Syndrome of Gonadal Dysgenesis)

• Most common X chromosome abnormality in ♀, affecting 1:2500 live ♀ births.

• Result of complete or partial absence of an X chromosome.

The classical form, 45,X0 karyotype represents 50% of all patients with X chromosome abnormalities, while structural rearrangement of the X chromosome, and/ or mosaicism: 45X0/46XX, 45X0/46XX/47XXX account for the rest.

7.7 Turner Syndrome (Syndrome of Gonadal Dysgenesis)

163

7.7.1 Clinical Presentation

The cardinal features of 45,X0 gonadal dysgenesis are a variety of somatic anomalies, sexual infantilism at puberty secondary to gonadal dysgenesis and short stature.

7.7.1.1 Somatic Anomalies

Patients with a 45,X karyotype can be recognized in infancy, usually because of lymphedema of the extremities, whereas later in life they are recognizable by typical facies: micrognathia, a fish-like mouth with a narrow, high-arched palate, hypertelorism, epicanthus, ptosis, strabismus, prominent, low-set ears, short, thick, and webbed neck; low posterior hairline, broad chest with widely spaced inverted nipples, multiple pigmented nevi, cubitus valgus (Madelung deformity of the wrist), short fourth metacarpals, and metatarsals have all been described in patients with Turner syndrome. There is an increased risk of celiac disease, autoimmune thyroiditis, DM, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, recurrent otitis media, cardiovascular defects—especially coarctation of aorta, nonstenotic bicuspid aorta, other left-sided congenital heart defects, and kidney anomalies. The most common renal anomalies are a horseshoe kidney, duplication of the renal pelvis and ureter, and hydronephrosis secondary to uteropelvic obstruction.

7.7.1.2 Short Stature

It is an invariable feature of the syndrome; mean final height in 45,X0 patients is 143 cm (mean: 133–153 cm). Note: Is not due to a deficiency of GH, IGF-I, sex steroids, or thyroid hormones; it is related, at least in part, to haploinsufficiency of the PHOG (pseudo-autosomal homeobox osteogenic gene)/SHOX (short stature homeobox gene) in the pseudo-­ autosomal region of the X.

7.7.1.3 Gonadal Dysgenesis

The gonads: ovarian follicles undergo premature apoptosis resulting in fibrous streaks as typical histologic finding. The genital tract and external genitalia are female in character but immature. Because ovarian function is impaired, puberty does not usually ensue spontaneously and hence, primary amenorrhea and sexual infantilism are hallmarks of this syndrome.

7.7.2 Laboratory Findings

• Hormonal evaluation: FSH, LH ↑ + ↓ E2

• X-ray findings: shortening of the fourth metacarpal, scoliosis

• Bone densitometry: osteoporosis

All patients with Turner syndrome should have a complete cardiac evaluation by a cardiologist at diagnosis as well as periodic follow-up echocardiography or MRI as necessary to monitor aortic diameter and cardiovascular status. Routine intravenous urography or renal sonography is also indicated to detect a surgically correctable renal abnormality. Ultrasonography of the pelvis or MRI: rudimentary ovaries/streak gonads, small uterus.

7.7.3 Diagnosis

• Barr test (determination of the X chromatin pattern (Barr body))—negative.

• Karyotype analysis is the definitive procedure: 45,X0/mosaicism.

7.7.4 Treatment

Objectives: therapy is directed toward maximizing final height and inducing secondary sexual characteristics and menarche at an age commensurate with that of normal peers. Although the short stature is not due to ↓ GH, administration of high-­ dose biosynthetic human GH results in an increase in final height.

• Give recombinant GH 45–50 μg/kg/day.

• In patients who have been treated with GH and have achieved an acceptable

height, estrogen replacement therapy should start between 11 and 12 years of age with low-dose, increasing to adult dosing over 2–3 years (the transdermal route is preferred), adding progesterone once breakthrough bleeding occurs, or after 2 years of estrogen treatment.

• Treat complications.

7.10 Klinefelter Syndrome (XXY Seminiferous Dysgenesis)

The most common congenital form of primary hypogonadism, occurring in 1 of 600 male births. The underlying defect is the presence of an extra X chromosome, the usual chromosomal karyotype being either 47XXY (classic form) or 46,XY/47,XXY (mosaic form). Clinical manifestations will depend on the age of diagnosis. Patients with mosaicism tend to have less severe clinical features.

• Histologic changes in the testes: hyalinization and fibrosis of the tubules, absence

of spermatogenesis ← obliteration of the seminiferous tubules; Leydig cells are also abnormal.

7.10.1 Clinical Presentation

The clinical manifestations of androgen deficiency vary considerably from patient to patient with Klinefelter syndrome and are related to the degree of diminished testosterone production and sometimes to alterations in the androgen receptor. Some untreated boys in their late teens and adult men have virtually no secondary sexual developmental changes, but others are indistinguishable from healthy individuals.

• ↑ Tall stature (↑ leg length); abnormal skeletal proportions that are not truly

eunuchoid (pubis-to-floor height is greater than crown-to-pubis height, but arm span is less than total height). Note: It is not secondary to androgen deficiency but is probably related to the underlying chromosomal abnormality.

• Small (<2 cm in longest axis, and 4 mL in volume), firm testes.

• Manifestations of androgen deficiency:

–– Gynecomastia (50%) –– Reduced libido and erectile dysfunction, reduced facial hair, infertility –– Penis and scrotum (during puberty) undergo varying degrees of development, with some individuals appearing normal! –– Osteoporosis

• In addition to symptoms and signs of male hypogonadism, boys and men with

Klinefelter syndrome have an increased prevalence of cognitive impairment (patients with three or more X chromosomes uniformly have severe cognitive impairment); learning disabilities, poor impulse control, feeling of inadequacy, and dissocial behavior are also common.

48,XXXY) or 46,XY/47,XXY mosaicism in the remainder.

variable degree of oligozoospermia).

7.10.3 Management

• It’s directed toward androgen replacement therapy.

• May need surgical reduction of gynecomastia.

• Fertility: intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), using testicular spermatozoa

from men with Klinefelter’s syndrome (sperm may be extracted directly from the testes in about half of the patients), has resulted in successful pregnancies with a live birth rate of up to 20%.

• However, couples should be counselled about the ↑ risk of chromosomal abnormalities in offspring.

7.11 Normal Sexual Differentiation

Fetal sexual development consists of three sequential stages:

1. An undifferentiated stage, characterized by the formation of gonadal and genitalia primordia, which are identical in both xx and XY embryos

2. Gonadal differentiation, where the undifferentiated gonads develop into ovaries

or testes

3. Sexual differentiation of the internal and external genitalia, which depends on

the existence or absence of male hormone action The genetic sex of the zygote is established by fertilization of a normal ovum by an X- or Y-bearing sperm, thus resulting in 46XX or 46 XY embryo.

7.11.1 Gonadal Development

• In the ♂ or ♀ embryo, the bipotential gonad develops as a thickening of mesenchymal cells and coelomic epithelium around the primitive kidney. This genital

ridge is then colonized by primordial germ cells which migrate from the yolk sac to form the gonadal ridge.

174

7

Reproductive Endocrinology

–– Under the influence of SRY—“the sex-determining region” on the Y chromosome/SOX9 and other genes that encode male sex determination, the undifferentiated and bipotential gonadal ridge begins to differentiate as a testis at 43–50 days of gestation. Hence immature Sertoli cells, germs cells, and seminiferous tubules can be recognized by 7 weeks, Leydig cells derived from steroidogenic cells are apparent by about 60 days and testis differentiation is complete by 9 weeks. –– In the absence of a Y chromosome and SRY gene expression and in the presence of the ovary specific genes (e.g., WNT4, RSPO1), the gonad will develop into an ovary. The onset of ovarian differentiation begins later-long after differentiation of the testes in the male fetus (at 77–84 days). Of note, the presence of germ cells is critical for the stabilization of the ovary, which is a major difference, as compared with testicular differentiation.

7.11.2 Internal Genitalia

By the seventh week of intrauterine life, the fetus is equipped with the primordia of both male and female genital ducts: the Wolffian ducts and the Mullerian structures.

• Embryonic Müllerian structures, if allowed to persist (in the absence of the testes, the wolffian ducts do not develop and the Mullerian structures differentiate)

form the uterus, Fallopian tubes, and upper third of the vagina. NB, female development is not contingent on the presence of an ovary, because development of the uterus and tubes occurs if no gonad is present!!!

• In ♂, anti-Müllerian hormone is secreted by immature Sertoli cells in the testis

by 6 weeks, and this causes regression of the Müllerian structures. Leydig cells produce testosterone under placental hCG stimulation. Testosterone promotes growth and differentiation of the Wolffian ducts to form the epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles and ejaculatory duct. NB, the influence of the fetal testis on duct development is exerted locally and unilaterally; if one testis is removed at an early stage of development, the oviduct develops normally on that side but Mullerian regression occurs on the side of the intact testis.

 ifferentiation of External Genitalia and Urogenital D Sinus

Up to the eighth week of life, the external genitalia of both sexes are identical and have the capacity to differentiate into the genitalia of either sex; they consist of a urogenital slit bounded by paired urethral folds and more laterally, by labioscrotal swellings, also called the genital swellings; the urogenital slit is surmounted by a genital tubercle consisting of corpora cavernosa and glans.

Normal Sexual Differentiation

175

• In the absence of any androgen secretion, labia majora, labia minora, and clitoris

develop from the embryonic genital swelling, genital fold, and genital tubercle, respectively. Female sex differentiation will occur in the presence of an ovary or streak gonads or if no gonad is present.

• Development of normal ♂ external genitalia requires testosterone production

from the testis and its conversion to DHT by the enzyme 5α-reductase. In the presence of DHT, the genital tubercle elongates to form the corpora cavernosa and glans penis; the urethral fold fuses and forms the penile shaft and the labioscrotal swelling fuses and forms the scrotum. This process commences around 9 weeks and is completed by 13 weeks. Testicular descent in ♂ occurs in the later two-thirds of gestation under control of fetal LH and testosterone. The lower vagina (lower 2/3 of the vagina) probably originate from the urogenital sinus (in normal female development, proliferation of the vesicovaginal septum pushes the vaginal orifice posteriorly so that it acquires a separate external opening). In ♂, DHT inhibits growth of the vesicovaginal septum, thereby preventing the development of the vagina, the vaginal pouch being usually obliterated when the Mullerian ducts are resorbed; the prostate gland and bulbourethral glands of Cowper in the male are outgrowths of the urogenital sinus. NB.

• Masculinization of the external genitalia and urogenital sinus of the fetus depend

on the action of T and particularly DHT and on the presence of the specific androgen receptor

• There is a critical period for action of the androgen!!!

1. Complete male differentiation of the external genitalia and urogenital sinus

occurs only if androgenic stimulus is received during the critical period of development (8–12 weeks) in fetal life.

2. After about the 12th week, when the vagina has separated from the urogenital
